items.definition: The smaller part of a currency, such as the cent of a dollar, that people rarely see.
items.example: The price is 12.50 dollars, but the money is made of dollars and cents.

items.definition: The value printed on a note or a coin, such as 20 or 500.
items.example: The shop keeps one drawer for the smallest denomination and one for the notes.

items.definition: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.
items.example: Ask which day the exchange rate belongs to, because the number is only true for that day.

items.definition: The currency of the pair that the rate counts from: one unit of it is the thing you exchange.
items.example: In EUR/USD the euro is the base currency and the dollar is the quote currency.

items.definition: The currency of the pair that the rate is expressed in, so the rate says how many units of it you get.
items.example: The rate is given in the quote currency, so a pair written EUR/USD reads in dollars.

items.definition: An arrangement in which several states use one currency and a single authority issues it for all of them.
items.example: The euro area is a currency union, so one central bank issues the notes for every member country.

items.definition: The use, by a country, of the currency of another country as its own money, with no domestic currency issued.
items.example: The country is dollarized: the shops take dollars and nobody issues local notes.

items.definition: The act of lowering the value that other people attach to a person's work or judgement.
items.example: The devaluation was quiet: every meeting began with a small doubt about her work.

items.definition: A country where most payments are still made in cash rather than by card or by transfer.
items.example: In a cash economy, a market stall may not have a machine at all.

items.definition: The market that trades a currency outside the official channel, at a rate the state does not set.
items.example: When the official rate stops working, the parallel market sets the real price of the dollar.

items.definition: The habit of adding a small sum on top of a bill for the person who served you.
items.example: In this restaurant the service charge is on the bill, so there is no tip to add.

items.definition: The money a person working abroad sends to the family at home.
items.example: He sends a remittance every month, and the rent is paid from it.

items.definition: The unit of time equal to one sixtieth of a minute.
The SI unit of force.
items.example: Newton’s second law, mechanical energy, Ohm’s law, and a travelling wave are written below.

items.definition: The capacity to do work or cause change.
The speed of a body together with its direction.
Matter of a definite kind and composition.
A written sign that stands for a quantity or an idea.
items.example: Read the symbol, then the English name.

items.definition: A short piece of text naming an item.
A level of quality or a rule of conduct.
A wrong result or a report of a fault.
An illustration, or a numerical value.
items.example: Use this when the title names one figure.

items.definition: The rate of change of velocity with time.
items.example: A car that speeds up from 0 to 100 km/h in 10 s has an acceleration of 2.78 m/s².

items.definition: The SI unit of amount of substance.
items.example: 18 g of water is about one mole.

items.definition: A dynamic state in which the forward and reverse rates are equal.
items.example: At equilibrium, the concentrations stay constant.

items.definition: The SI unit of electrical resistance.
items.example: A 2 Ω resistor carries 3 A when V = 6 V.

items.definition: A form of English used by a particular group in a particular place, with its own vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.
items.example: Singapore English is a variety of English, not a broken version of it.

items.definition: The way the sounds of a language are pronounced by a speaker, independent of which words they use.
items.example: He has a strong Glasgow accent but standard vocabulary.

items.definition: Whether a speaker pronounces the r sound at the end of a word. American English is rhotic; British English is not.
items.example: The difference between *car* and *cah* is rhoticity.

items.definition: The level of formality a speaker chooses for a situation, from casual to formal.
items.example: Switching register, he changed *Could you pass the salt* to *Pass the salt*.

items.definition: Moving between two languages, or two varieties of one language, inside a single conversation.
items.example: Code-switching between English and Tamil is normal in Chennai offices.

items.definition: A shared language used between people whose first languages differ. English is the most common one in international business.
items.example: English works as the lingua franca, so nobody has to learn three languages for one meeting.

items.definition: The individual version of a language: one speaker's own habits of words and grammar.
items.example: Every email you write becomes part of your idiolect.

items.definition: Someone who earns income that does not depend on one country and who lives in several places over a year.
items.example: As a digital nomad, I move when the client contract ends.

items.definition: A residence permit for people who work remotely for foreign employers or clients without a local work permit.
items.example: The nomad visa requires proof of income above a monthly threshold.

items.definition: The status that decides which country has a claim to tax your income, usually based on where you spend most of your time.
items.example: Tax residency is the part nobody checks before they book the flight.

items.definition: A building where residents rent a room and share a kitchen and common areas, and where nomads often find a community.
items.example: I took a room in a coliving for a month and made friends in a week.

items.definition: A paid workspace where people work in the same room, usually by the day or the month, with a desk and reliable internet.
items.example: A co-working space costs less than the coffee I would buy sitting in a café all day.

items.definition: Staying in one place for weeks or months instead of moving on every few days, which is what makes long-term work possible.
items.example: Slow travel costs less and lets you actually know the place.

items.definition: Working from a shared space other than your own home, which many employers offer or pay for.
items.example: My company gave me an offsiting budget of two hundred dollars a month.
